title: Reading a Turnkey House Construction Quote: Items Often Left Out
desc: A low turnkey quote is not necessarily cheap. Items often left out, how to read the scope, materials and taxes, and how to prevent extra costs from the start.
summary: How to read a turnkey house construction quote to avoid extra costs: check the scope of work, material types, taxes and fees, and items often left out.
body: p

Two lump-sum quotes that differ by several hundred million dong do not necessarily mean the lower one is cheaper. In many cases a quote is low because it leaves out items, and then charges extra costs during construction. This article helps you read a quote before signing.
h2
1. What does “lump-sum (turnkey)” mean under the law?
p

A lump-sum contract has a price fixed at signing that does not change throughout performance, corresponding to the content and scope of work agreed, except in force majeure, fundamental change of circumstances, a change in the scope of work, or other cases the parties agree on (Point a, Clause 2, Article 6 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP). So a “lump-sum” price is only firm when the scope of work is fully and clearly stated. Any item not in the quote becomes an extra cost if added later.
p
Other types of contract price are explained in Types of construction contract price.
h2
2. Three things a quote must contain
ul
Scope and quantities of work according to the design drawings (Article 8). The quote should attach the drawings or clearly state which drawings it is based on.
Material types: brand, specification, grade, size, and ceiling unit price for floor and wall tiles, sanitary fixtures, doors, paint, electrical wire and water pipes.
Taxes and fees included or not – the law requires the parties to clearly agree on the costs, taxes, fees and charges included and not included in the contract price (Clause 2, Article 11).
h2
3. Items often omitted
ol
Foundation reinforcement, pile driving or bored piles on weak soil; excavation and hauling away surplus soil.
Demolition of the old house, site clearance, and shoring of adjoining houses.
Waterproofing of bathroom floors, the rooftop terrace, the roof, and walls adjoining the neighboring house.
Underground water tank, septic tank, manholes, and drainage to the public sewer.
Electrical and plumbing: number of sockets and switches, network cable, air-conditioner piping, hot water lines.
Railings, stair handrails, roof covers, protective frames, gates and fences.
Exterior paint, how high wall tiling goes, and whether there is a plasterboard ceiling.
Construction electricity and water, protective netting, removal of waste, and cleaning at handover.
h2
4. The trap of the word “equivalent” and ceiling unit prices
p

A quote that says “equivalent tiles” or “mid-range sanitary fixtures” is easy to dispute. It is better to state specific product names or a ceiling unit price (for example, tiles not exceeding X dong/m²); if the owner chooses a more expensive type, only the difference is paid. This agreement should be written in the contract as the basis for payment.
h2
5. Preventing extra costs from the contract stage
ul
State clearly: reasonable additional quantities and work must have the unit price, or the method of calculating the unit price, agreed by both parties before being carried out (Clause 3, Article 23).
Make all proposals and requests during construction in writing or in saved messages (Clause 4, Article 4).
Attach the materials list and drawings as contract appendices – see Residential construction contracts: what they should contain.
h2
6. Tip for comparing 2–3 quotes
p

Make a table: each row is an item, each column is a contractor. For any item that one side has and the other does not, ask again or estimate the addition. Compare the totals only after bringing the quotes to the same scope. If you need an independent party to review the quotes, you can contact Quan Construction.
note

This article is for reference only and is not financial or legal advice. Decree 210/2026/ND-CP applies to construction contracts; its specific levels are mandatory only for projects using state funds and PPP projects, while private housing contracts are mainly agreed by the two parties under the Civil Code.
